title: ServiceRegistryProxyGeneric exposes all service management functions without access control
description: The ServiceRegistryProxyGeneric contract acts as the manager of ServiceRegistryF (since the proxy deploys it and the ServiceRegistryF constructor sets owner=msg.sender, which is the proxy). The proxy then calls management functions on ServiceRegistryF. However, ALL functions in ServiceRegistryProxyGeneric (create, update, activateRegistration, registerAgents, deploy, terminate, unbond, slash, changeOwner, changeManager, changeDrainer, changeMultisigPermission) have NO access control modifiers. Any external caller can invoke these functions freely, bypassing the intended manager-only restriction that ServiceRegistryF enforces at the registry level (it only checks msg.sender == manager, which is the proxy address). Since any EOA can call the proxy, the manager check in ServiceRegistryF is completely bypassed.
message: Any attacker can create arbitrary services with any parameters, terminate services to steal security deposits, unbond operators to claim bonds, change the owner/manager/drainer of the registry, whitelist malicious multisig implementations, or drain slashed funds to arbitrary addresses.
recommendation: Add an owner state variable to ServiceRegistryProxyGeneric and restrict all administrative/mutating functions with an onlyOwner modifier. Alternatively, the proxy should set the ServiceRegistryF's manager to a separate trusted EOA/multisig rather than leaving all proxy functions open. Example: add `address public proxyOwner; modifier onlyProxyOwner() { require(msg.sender == proxyOwner, 'Not owner'); _; }` and apply it to all state-changing proxy functions.
exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker calls proxy.create(attackerAddress, validConfigHash, agentIds, agentParams, threshold) - service is created with attacker as owner. 2. Attacker calls proxy.activateRegistration{value: securityDeposit}(attackerAddress, serviceId). 3. Attacker calls proxy.terminate(attackerAddress, serviceId) to get refund. 4. Separately: attacker calls proxy.changeOwner(attackerAddress) which calls iServiceRegistryF.changeOwner(attackerAddress) - since proxy IS the current owner, this succeeds, giving attacker full ownership of ServiceRegistryF. 5. Attacker can then call proxy.changeDrainer(attackerAddress) and proxy.drain() to steal all slashed funds.

title: Security deposit not zeroed before ETH transfer in terminate(), enabling double-refund if state allows re-entry through non-guarded paths
description: In the terminate() function, `refund = service.securityDeposit` is read and immediately sent via `serviceOwner.call{value: refund}('')` but `service.securityDeposit` is never set to zero after the transfer. While the reentrancy guard (_locked) prevents direct re-entry into terminate(), the service state is set to PreRegistration (when numAgentInstances == 0), allowing the service owner to call activateRegistration again with the same securityDeposit amount. The protocol assumes securityDeposit is a per-activation deposit, but since it persists in the struct, repeated terminate/activate cycles will continuously refund the security deposit from contract balance while that ETH was only deposited once.
message: A service owner can repeatedly cycle through activateRegistration -> terminate to drain ETH from the contract. Each cycle: pay securityDeposit, get it back. However if another service's deposit is in the contract, the accounting can break causing the contract to owe more ETH than it holds.
recommendation: Set `service.securityDeposit = 0` after computing the refund but before the external call: `refund = service.securityDeposit; service.securityDeposit = 0; (bool result,) = serviceOwner.call{value: refund}('');`
exploit_scenario: 1. Create service with securityDeposit = X ETH. 2. Call activateRegistration with X ETH - contract now holds X ETH. 3. Call terminate - refund X ETH back, service goes to PreRegistration state, securityDeposit still = X in struct. 4. This is correct for a single cycle. However: if service.securityDeposit is updated in a subsequent update() call to a LOWER value, the stored securityDeposit in the struct changes, but the actual ETH held for this service was the original amount. The mismatch between stored securityDeposit (post-update) and actual ETH held (pre-update value) means terminate() refunds less than deposited, permanently locking ETH in the contract.

title: update() can change securityDeposit after ETH is locked, causing ETH to be permanently locked or refund shortfall
description: The update() function can only be called when service.state == PreRegistration. However, after a service is terminated with numAgentInstances > 0 -> TerminatedBonded -> unbond all -> PreRegistration, the service returns to PreRegistration. At this point, update() can be called to change agentParams (and thus securityDeposit). The securityDeposit stored in the service struct is recomputed by _setServiceData() as the maximum bond across all agent params. If this new securityDeposit differs from what was paid during the previous activateRegistration cycle, the ETH accounting breaks. More critically: the service struct is stored as `Service memory service` in update() and then written back via `mapServices[serviceId] = service`, which overwrites the entire struct including securityDeposit. But no ETH adjustment is made. The next activateRegistration will require the NEW securityDeposit amount, but no reconciliation of old ETH is performed.
message: If securityDeposit increases, the service owner must pay more in the next activation - this is intended. But if securityDeposit decreases, the terminate() function will refund the LOWER (new) amount even if the higher amount was paid, permanently locking the difference in the contract with no withdrawal mechanism.
recommendation: Track ETH deposited separately from the computed securityDeposit, or ensure that update() can only change securityDeposit when no ETH is held (i.e., only from fresh PreRegistration, not post-unbond PreRegistration). Add an explicit ETH accounting variable per service.
exploit_scenario: 1. Create service with agentParams bond=10 ETH (securityDeposit=10). 2. activateRegistration with 10 ETH. 3. terminate() - refunds 10 ETH, state->PreRegistration, securityDeposit still 10 in struct (correct here). 4. update() with new agentParams bond=5 ETH - _setServiceData sets securityDeposit=5. 5. activateRegistration with 5 ETH. 6. terminate() refunds only 5 ETH. Net: 5 ETH locked in contract forever with no recovery function.

title: serviceId bit-packing with operatorService key truncates serviceId > 2^32-1, causing key collisions
description: The operatorService key is constructed as: `uint256 operatorService = uint256(uint160(operator)); operatorService |= serviceId << 160;`. The comment states 'serviceId occupies next 32 bits assuming it is not greater than 2^32 - 1 in value'. However, totalSupply is a uint256 and there is no cap enforced. If serviceId > 2^32-1 (i.e., > 4,294,967,295), the shifted bits will overflow into bits beyond position 192 and wrap, causing collisions between different (operator, serviceId) pairs. The same truncation issue exists for the serviceAgent key: `serviceAgent |= uint256(agentIds[i]) << 32` where agentIds are uint32 so this is safe, but serviceId is used as the lower 32 bits which is also safe for serviceId <= 2^32-1. However totalSupply has no upper bound check.
message: After 4 billion services are created, key collisions in mapOperatorAndServiceIdAgentInstances, mapOperatorAndServiceIdOperatorBalances would allow operators to access other operators' bond balances or agent instance records, enabling theft of bonded ETH.
recommendation: Add a check in create(): `if (serviceId > type(uint32).max) revert Overflow(serviceId, type(uint32).max);` or refactor the key packing to use keccak256(abi.encode(operator, serviceId)) for collision-free keys.
exploit_scenario: If serviceId = 2^32 (4294967296), then serviceId << 160 has bit 192 set. A different serviceId = 0 with a different operator whose address has bit 32 set would produce the same key. While 4B services is unlikely, the lack of enforcement is a design flaw.

title: Reentrancy via onERC721Received callback during _safeMint in create() before state is fully committed
description: In ServiceRegistryF.create(), the sequence is: (1) increment totalSupply, (2) write service data to mapServices, (3) call _safeMint(serviceOwner, serviceId). The _safeMint calls onERC721Received on the serviceOwner if it's a contract. At this point, _locked = 2 so direct reentrancy into create() is blocked. However, the callback can call OTHER non-locked functions like update(), getService(), or even interact with the proxy's unprotected functions. More critically, since the proxy has NO reentrancy guard itself and forwards calls to ServiceRegistryF, a malicious serviceOwner contract receiving the NFT via onERC721Received could call proxy functions that are NOT protected by _locked in ServiceRegistryF (e.g., functions that don't have the reentrancy guard like slash(), update()). The service exists in mapServices at this point but in PreRegistration state, so update() would succeed if called from the callback since state==PreRegistration check passes.
message: A malicious serviceOwner can use the onERC721Received callback to call update() and modify the just-created service's parameters (agentIds, agentParams, configHash) before the create() transaction completes, potentially setting a lower securityDeposit to reduce future activation costs or changing the service configuration.
recommendation: Move the _safeMint call to after all state is committed AND move _locked = 1 reset to after _safeMint, or use _mint instead of _safeMint. Alternatively, ensure update() also acquires the reentrancy lock.
exploit_scenario: 1. Deploy MaliciousOwner contract that implements onERC721Received. 2. In onERC721Received, call proxy.update(address(this), newConfigHash, newAgentIds, cheaperAgentParams, newThreshold, serviceId). 3. This succeeds because service.state == PreRegistration. 4. The service is now created with the original params in the event but stored with manipulated params.

title: Hardcoded Multisig Implementation in Proxy Bypasses Authorization
description: The `ServiceRegistryProxy.deploy` function ignores the `multisigImplementation` parameter passed by the caller and hardcodes the address `0x48BaCB9266a570d521063EF5dD96e61686DbE788` when forwarding to `ServiceRegistryF.deploy`. This means any caller can deploy a service using this specific multisig implementation regardless of what they pass. More critically, this bypasses any intended permission system where different multisig implementations should be selectable. If the hardcoded address is later removed from `mapMultisigs` (via `changeMultisigPermission`), all proxy-based deployments will fail permanently.
message: Users cannot choose their multisig implementation through the proxy. If the hardcoded multisig is dewhitelisted, the proxy's deploy function breaks entirely. Additionally, if the hardcoded address is malicious or compromised, all services deployed through the proxy use it.
recommendation: Pass the `multisigImplementation` parameter through: `return iServiceRegistryF.deploy(serviceOwner, serviceId, multisigImplementation, data);` and remove the hardcoded address.
exploit_scenario: 1. Call `ServiceRegistryProxy.deploy(owner, serviceId, anyAddress, data)` - the `anyAddress` parameter is silently ignored. 2. The call always uses `0x48BaCB9266a570d521063EF5dD96e61686DbE788` as multisig implementation. 3. If owner calls `changeMultisigPermission(0x48BaCB9266a570d521063EF5dD96e61686DbE788, false)`, all proxy deploy calls revert with `UnauthorizedMultisig`.

title: Security Deposit Not Zeroed After terminate() - Potential Double Refund
description: In `terminate()`, the security deposit (`service.securityDeposit`) is refunded to `serviceOwner` but `service.securityDeposit` is never set to zero in the storage struct. The function reads `refund = service.securityDeposit` from a `Service storage service` and sends it, but never does `service.securityDeposit = 0`. If the service re-enters `PreRegistration` state (when `numAgentInstances == 0`), then `activateRegistration` can be called again with the same deposit amount. However, crucially, if somehow terminate is called again (which is currently protected by state checks), the deposit would be double-refunded from contract balance.
message: While the state machine prevents immediate double-refund (terminate checks state != PreRegistration && state != TerminatedBonded), the securityDeposit persists in storage incorrectly. When the service is re-activated via `activateRegistration`, it requires paying the same deposit again (correct), but the stored value from a previous cycle is still there, creating accounting inconsistency. A more severe issue: if a service owner terminates while in `ActiveRegistration` (numAgentInstances == 0), they get refunded AND the service goes back to PreRegistration with the same securityDeposit value stored - they never paid it again but it shows as if they did.
recommendation: Add `service.securityDeposit = 0;` after the refund in `terminate()`, and restore it in `activateRegistration()` if needed for re-use.
exploit_scenario: 1. Create service, activate registration (pay securityDeposit). 2. Call terminate() with no agents registered (numAgentInstances == 0). 3. Service state -> PreRegistration, securityDeposit refunded. 4. service.securityDeposit still shows the old value in storage. 5. Call activateRegistration again - must pay securityDeposit again (correct). 6. Call terminate again - refunded again correctly. The issue is the stale storage value could cause issues in downstream accounting or view functions that read securityDeposit.

title: serviceId Bit-Packing Overflow: serviceId > 2^96 Causes Key Collision
description: In `registerAgents()`, the key for `mapOperatorAndServiceIdOperatorBalances` and `mapOperatorAndServiceIdAgentInstances` is computed as: `uint256 operatorService = uint256(uint160(operator)); operatorService |= serviceId << 160;`. If `serviceId >= 2^96`, the shift `serviceId << 160` will overflow (since serviceId is uint256, and 160+96=256 bits), causing the upper bits of serviceId to be lost. This leads to key collisions between services with IDs that differ only in the upper 96 bits. Similarly in `slash()`, same packing is used.
message: If totalSupply of services exceeds 2^96 (extremely unlikely in practice but theoretically possible), operator balances for different services would collide, allowing operators to claim refunds from wrong services or have balances incorrectly slashed.
recommendation: Add a check that serviceId <= type(uint96).max, or use a different key encoding (e.g., keccak256(abi.encodePacked(operator, serviceId))).
exploit_scenario: If serviceId_A = X and serviceId_B = X + 2^96, then `serviceId_A << 160` and `serviceId_B << 160` produce the same result (overflow), causing key collision in operator balance mappings.

title: Reentrancy in create() via _safeMint Before State Finalization
description: In `ServiceRegistryF.create()`, `_safeMint(serviceOwner, serviceId)` is called after `totalSupply = serviceId` is set and `mapServices[serviceId] = service` is stored. The `_safeMint` calls `onERC721Received` on contract recipients. While the reentrancy guard `_locked = 2` prevents direct reentrance into `create()`, it does NOT prevent reentrance into other non-guarded functions like `update()`, `activateRegistration()`, or state-reading functions. An attacker's `onERC721Received` callback could call `update()` on the newly created service (since it's already in storage) before `_locked` is reset to 1.
message: A malicious service owner (contract) can modify the newly created service's configuration during the `onERC721Received` callback in `create()`. Since `update()` has no reentrancy guard, the service configuration could be altered immediately after creation but within the same transaction.
recommendation: Add reentrancy guard to `update()` function, or move `_safeMint` to after all state changes and ensure `_locked` is restored before external calls. Consider using checks-effects-interactions pattern more strictly.
exploit_scenario: 1. Deploy malicious contract that implements `onERC721Received`. 2. Call `create()` with malicious contract as `serviceOwner`. 3. `_safeMint` calls `maliciousContract.onERC721Received`. 4. Inside callback, call `update(serviceOwner, newConfigHash, newAgentIds, newAgentParams, newThreshold, serviceId)`. 5. Service is updated to attacker's desired config before `create()` completes. 6. Manager may be unaware the service was modified.

title: terminate() Sends ETH Before Resetting State (Reentrancy via serviceOwner)
description: In `terminate()`, the function sends ETH to `serviceOwner` via `serviceOwner.call{value: refund}('')` but the reentrancy guard `_locked = 2` prevents direct re-entry into `terminate()` itself. However, `_locked` is set to 2 at the start. The ETH transfer happens BEFORE `_locked = 1` is reset. During the callback, `serviceOwner` (if a contract) cannot call `terminate()` again due to the lock, BUT can call `unbond()` which has its own reentrancy guard. The more serious issue: the service state is set to either `PreRegistration` or `TerminatedBonded` BEFORE the ETH transfer, so state is correct. However, `service.securityDeposit` is not zeroed, and if the call fails and reverts, the entire transaction reverts - but if the call succeeds and then a sub-call within the ETH transfer causes issues, there's a potential issue with how delete operations work in combination with the ETH send.
message: Limited direct impact due to reentrancy guard, but the combination of non-zeroed securityDeposit and ETH transfer to arbitrary address creates risk if state machine invariants are violated through creative transaction ordering.
recommendation: Zero out `service.securityDeposit` before the ETH transfer. Follow checks-effects-interactions: complete all state changes before external calls.
exploit_scenario: The reentrancy guard on terminate() prevents direct double-terminate. The main risk is that serviceOwner receives ETH callback and can interact with other unguarded functions while terminate's _locked=2 is active.

title: Proxy Functions Forward msg.sender as Operator/Owner Without Validation
description: The `ServiceRegistryProxy` forwards sensitive parameters like `serviceOwner`, `operator` directly from calldata to `ServiceRegistryF` without verifying that `msg.sender` is actually the claimed `serviceOwner` or `operator`. For example, `terminate(address serviceOwner, uint256 serviceId)` - any user can call this on the proxy with any `serviceOwner` address. The proxy doesn't check `msg.sender == serviceOwner`. In `ServiceRegistryF.terminate()`, the manager check passes because the proxy IS the manager. The ownership check `ownerOf(serviceId) != serviceOwner` provides some protection, but an attacker can still call `terminate` with the real owner's address, triggering termination and sending refunds to the real owner (griefing). Similarly `unbond(address operator, ...)` can be called by anyone specifying any operator.
message: Anyone can call `terminate()` through the proxy by supplying the correct service owner address, causing premature service termination. While the refund goes to the legitimate owner, this is a griefing attack that forces service owners to go through the full re-activation cycle. For `registerAgents`, anyone can register agents on behalf of any operator, potentially forcing operators to bond ETH they didn't intend to.
recommendation: Add `require(msg.sender == serviceOwner, 'Not owner')` checks in the proxy for functions that take owner/operator as parameters, or redesign the proxy to use `msg.sender` directly rather than accepting these as parameters.
exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker knows serviceId=5 is owned by Alice. 2. Attacker calls `ServiceRegistryProxy.terminate(aliceAddress, 5)`. 3. Proxy calls `ServiceRegistryF.terminate(aliceAddress, 5)` with proxy as msg.sender (manager). 4. ServiceRegistryF verifies proxy is manager (passes) and that ownerOf(5)==aliceAddress (passes). 5. Service is terminated, refund sent to Alice, but against Alice's wishes.

title: update() Lacks Reentrancy Guard
description: The `update()` function in `ServiceRegistryF` modifies service state including `mapServiceAndAgentIdAgentParams` (deleting entries for zero-slot agents) but has no reentrancy guard. While it doesn't directly handle ETH, it can be called from within a reentrant context (e.g., during `_safeMint`'s `onERC721Received` callback in `create()`). Additionally, if `_initialChecks` calls `IRegistry(agentRegistry).totalSupply()` on an untrusted registry, a malicious registry could reenter.
message: State inconsistency if update() is called reentrantly during create(). Service configuration could be modified mid-creation.
recommendation: Add reentrancy guard to `update()`: check and set `_locked` at start and end of function.
exploit_scenario: 1. Set manager to malicious contract. 2. Malicious manager calls create(), which calls _safeMint to a malicious serviceOwner contract. 3. serviceOwner's onERC721Received calls update() (since create()'s _locked=2 only blocks create(), not update()). 4. update() modifies the just-created service's agent params.

title: Wrong Manager Check in refundFromStaking Uses depository Instead of dispenser in Error
description: The refundFromStaking function checks `if (dispenser != msg.sender)` correctly but then emits the error with `depository` as the required manager: `revert ManagerOnly(msg.sender, depository)`. This is a logic error in the error reporting but not a security issue itself. However, more critically, this function is supposed to only be callable by dispenser but reports wrong address.
message: Minor incorrect error reporting, but could confuse debugging. Not a fund loss vulnerability.
recommendation: Change `revert ManagerOnly(msg.sender, depository)` to `revert ManagerOnly(msg.sender, dispenser)`
exploit_scenario: Call refundFromStaking from a non-dispenser address; the error will show depository as required manager instead of dispenser.

title: Division by Zero in _finalizeIncentivesForUnitId When sumUnitTopUpsOLAS Is Zero
description: In `_finalizeIncentivesForUnitId`, when calculating topUp incentives, the code computes `sumUnitIncentives = uint256(mapEpochTokenomics[epochNum].unitPoints[unitType].sumUnitTopUpsOLAS) * 100` and then divides `totalIncentives / sumUnitIncentives`. If `sumUnitTopUpsOLAS` is zero (which can happen if no eligible service donated or topUpUnitFraction was zero), this causes a division by zero panic, reverting all transactions that attempt to finalize incentives for such units. However, the outer `if (totalIncentives > 0)` check on `pendingRelativeTopUp` should prevent this case - if pendingRelativeTopUp > 0 then sumUnitTopUpsOLAS should also be > 0. BUT: consider a race condition where `sumUnitTopUpsOLAS` overflows to zero due to accumulation in uint96, OR if tokenomics parameters were manipulated. More critically, in the `getOwnerIncentives` view function, the same calculation is done without this protection being guaranteed.
message: Potential DoS for incentive claiming if sumUnitTopUpsOLAS is manipulated to zero while pendingRelativeTopUp is non-zero
recommendation: Add explicit check: `if (sumUnitIncentives == 0) { mapUnitIncentives[unitType][unitId].pendingRelativeTopUp = 0; } else { ... division ... }`. Also apply to getOwnerIncentives.
exploit_scenario: 1. Unit accumulates pendingRelativeTopUp during epoch N. 2. Through parameter manipulation or edge case, sumUnitTopUpsOLAS[N] becomes 0. 3. When _finalizeIncentivesForUnitId(N, ...) is called, division by zero reverts. 4. Unit owner permanently locked out of incentives.

title: effectiveBond Can Exceed Inflation Budget Due to Unbounded Accumulation
description: At the end of `checkpoint()`, the code does `curMaxBond += effectiveBond; effectiveBond = uint96(curMaxBond)`. This accumulates the maxBond into effectiveBond every epoch. If bond programs don't use the full effectiveBond, it keeps growing. Over many epochs with low bond utilization, `effectiveBond` can grow to exceed `type(uint96).max`, causing an overflow revert. More seriously, the `refundFromBondProgram` adds back to `effectiveBond`, and combined with the per-epoch addition of maxBond, the effectiveBond can far exceed the actual available OLAS inflation, allowing more bonds to be issued than there is OLAS inflation to back them. The overflow check `if (eBond > type(uint96).max) revert Overflow(...)` in `refundFromBondProgram` is good, but in `checkpoint` the addition `curMaxBond += effectiveBond` can silently overflow uint256 to wrap, then truncate to uint96.
message: Bond programs could be backed by more OLAS than actually available in inflation, potentially causing OLAS minting to exceed inflation caps, leading to insolvency.
recommendation: Cap effectiveBond at a reasonable maximum (e.g., related to annual inflation). Add: `if (curMaxBond > MAX_EFFECTIVE_BOND) curMaxBond = MAX_EFFECTIVE_BOND; effectiveBond = uint96(curMaxBond);`
exploit_scenario: 1. Deploy with large maxBondFraction (50%). 2. Over many epochs, never fully utilize bond programs. 3. effectiveBond accumulates: effectiveBond(n+1) = effectiveBond(n) + maxBond(n+1). 4. After enough epochs, effectiveBond >> actual available OLAS. 5. Bond programs can be created for amounts backed by non-existent OLAS inflation.

title: Reentrancy Risk in _trackServiceDonations Via External Calls Before State Finalization
description: In `_trackServiceDonations`, multiple external calls are made: `IToken(serviceRegistry).ownerOf()`, `IVotingEscrow(ve).getVotes()`, and `IServiceRegistry(serviceRegistry).getUnitIdsOfService()`. These are called within a loop. The `_locked` reentrancy guard is set during initialization but there is NO reentrancy guard on `trackServiceDonations` itself. The function is called from treasury, which is trusted, BUT if `serviceRegistry`, `ve`, or `componentRegistry`/`agentRegistry` contracts are compromised or have callbacks, they could reenter `trackServiceDonations` or `checkpoint` during processing. Furthermore, `IToken(registries[unitType]).ownerOf(serviceUnitIds[j])` is called for each unit - if the registry contract has a malicious callback or reenters, it could manipulate state mid-loop. The `_locked` variable exists but is never checked in any function.
message: Reentrancy could allow double-counting of donations or manipulation of unit incentive accounting.
recommendation: Add reentrancy guard modifier using the `_locked` variable that is already defined but never used as a guard. Add `modifier nonReentrant` and apply to `trackServiceDonations`, `checkpoint`, and `accountOwnerIncentives`.
exploit_scenario: 1. Malicious serviceRegistry returns a callback on ownerOf. 2. Callback reenters trackServiceDonations with different amounts. 3. State is modified mid-processing of original call. 4. Incentive accounting becomes inconsistent.

title: Existing _locked Variable Never Used as Reentrancy Guard
description: The contract declares `uint8 internal _locked` and sets it to `1` in `initializeTokenomics`, clearly intending it to be a reentrancy guard. However, it is NEVER used to protect any function. No function checks `_locked` before execution or sets it to `2` during execution. This means the reentrancy guard mechanism is completely non-functional. The state-changing functions `trackServiceDonations`, `checkpoint`, and `accountOwnerIncentives` all make external calls and have no reentrancy protection despite the guard variable existing.
message: All state-changing functions with external calls are vulnerable to reentrancy. Specifically, `accountOwnerIncentives` clears balances after calculating rewards - a reentrant call could claim rewards multiple times before balances are cleared.
recommendation: Implement the reentrancy guard: `modifier nonReentrant() { require(_locked == 1, 'Reentrant'); _locked = 2; _; _locked = 1; }` and apply it to trackServiceDonations, checkpoint, and accountOwnerIncentives.
exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker owns component/agent units. 2. Calls accountOwnerIncentives through dispenser. 3. During `IToken(registries[unitTypes[i]]).ownerOf(unitIds[i])` call, malicious registry reenters accountOwnerIncentives. 4. Rewards are accumulated again before being cleared. 5. Double (or more) rewards extracted.

title: trackServiceDonations Does Not Validate amounts Array Values Are Non-Zero
description: The `trackServiceDonations` function accepts `amounts` array from treasury without validating individual array entries are non-zero or that they match the actual ETH sent. Specifically, `donationETH` is the sum passed in, but individual `amounts[i]` values are trusted without cross-validation against `donationETH`. An attacker who controls the treasury (or a compromised treasury) could pass amounts[i] values that sum to more than donationETH, causing `pendingRelativeReward` and `pendingRelativeTopUp` to be inflated beyond what ETH was actually donated. More critically: `amounts[i] / numServiceUnits` uses integer division which truncates, so the sum of truncated amounts could be less than donationETH, creating an accounting discrepancy where totalDonationsETH > sum of all pending incentive amounts.
message: Accounting discrepancy between totalDonationsETH and actual per-unit incentive amounts, leading to some ETH being unclaimable (locked in treasury) or over-allocation of rewards.
recommendation: This is a known precision loss due to integer division. Consider accumulating remainder or use a different accounting method. At minimum, document this known precision loss.
exploit_scenario: 1. Donate to service with 3 units, amount = 100 wei. 2. Each unit gets 100/3 = 33 wei. 3. Total distributed = 99 wei, but totalDonationsETH += 100. 4. 1 wei per service donation is permanently unclaimable.

title: initializeTokenomics Has No Access Control - Can Be Front-Run
description: The `initializeTokenomics` function only checks `if (owner != address(0)) revert AlreadyInitialized()`. This means the very FIRST call sets `owner = msg.sender`. In a proxy deployment scenario, if the proxy is deployed but `initializeTokenomics` hasn't been called yet, ANY attacker can front-run the initialization transaction and call `initializeTokenomics` with their own address as `owner` and malicious contract addresses for treasury, depository, dispenser, etc. The attacker would become owner and control all tokenomics parameters. This is a classic proxy initialization front-running attack.
message: Attacker becomes owner of the tokenomics contract, controls all parameters, can redirect funds, manipulate inflation, and compromise the entire protocol.
recommendation: Use a constructor-based initialization lock or add an immutable deployer address check. Alternatively, use OpenZeppelin's Initializable with a deployer check, or include the expected owner as a constructor argument to the proxy.
exploit_scenario: 1. Protocol deploys proxy pointing to Tokenomics implementation. 2. Before deploying team calls initializeTokenomics, attacker sees the pending tx in mempool. 3. Attacker front-runs with higher gas, calling initializeTokenomics with their address and malicious contract addresses. 4. Attacker is now owner, can set treasury to their address, manipulate all parameters.

title: Wrong Address in Error for refundFromStaking Access Control Check
description: In `refundFromStaking`, the access control check reads: `if (dispenser != msg.sender) { revert ManagerOnly(msg.sender, depository); }`. The condition correctly checks against `dispenser`, but the revert error incorrectly passes `depository` as the required manager. More critically, this error in the error message suggests a copy-paste error that could mask a deeper logic error: the function is supposed to be called by dispenser to return staking OLAS, and if the wrong address was intended in the condition itself (e.g., if it should check depository instead), it would mean the wrong contract controls staking refunds. If this was meant to be controlled by depository (bond contract) instead of dispenser, then the wrong entity has control over inflating the staking incentive pool.
message: If the condition was meant to check depository (not dispenser), then the dispenser can arbitrarily inflate `mapEpochStakingPoints[eCounter].stakingIncentive` beyond the actual allocated amount, potentially causing the staking system to distribute more OLAS than allocated by inflation.
recommendation: Fix the error: `revert ManagerOnly(msg.sender, dispenser)`. Verify the intended caller is indeed dispenser and not depository. Add a cap ensuring refunded amount <= previously allocated staking amount for the epoch.
exploit_scenario: 1. Assuming dispenser is the correct caller (not depository): dispenser calls refundFromStaking(largeAmount). 2. stakingIncentive for current epoch increases by largeAmount. 3. At checkpoint, this inflated stakingIncentive is used as the base for further staking allocation. 4. More OLAS distributed to staking than allocated by inflation.

title: Missing reentrancy guard on activateRegistration and registerAgents payable functions
description: These payable functions lack reentrancy protection. While they don't make external calls, they accept ETH and change state. However, since all callers must be the manager (trusted), the immediate risk is limited.
message: Low direct impact given manager trust assumption
recommendation: Add reentrancy guard for defense-in-depth
exploit_scenario: N/A

title: Slash function does not verify agent instances belong to the target service
description: The slash() function accepts agentInstances and a serviceId, but never verifies that the provided agent instances are actually registered in the specified service. It only looks up mapAgentInstanceOperators[agentInstance] to get the operator, then constructs the operatorService key using the CALLER's serviceId. This means the multisig of service B can pass agent instances from service A to identify an operator O, then slash O's balance in service B—even though those agent instances have no relation to service B.
message: A malicious service multisig can slash operators using agent instances from other services, bypassing the intended constraint that only instances registered in the service can be used for slashing.
recommendation: Add a verification step: check that agentInstances[i] is in mapServiceAndAgentIdAgentInstances for the given serviceId, or check that mapAgentInstanceOperators[agentInstance] has a valid entry for this specific service.
exploit_scenario: 1. Operator O registers agent instance AI_A in service A and AI_B in service B. 2. Service B's multisig is malicious. 3. Multisig calls slash([AI_A], [fullAmount], serviceB_id). 4. mapAgentInstanceOperators[AI_A] = O. 5. operatorService = O | serviceB_id<<160. 6. O's service B balance is slashed using service A's agent instance. While damage equals what the multisig could do with legitimate instances, it bypasses accounting integrity.

title: Reentrancy via _safeMint callback in create() can invoke unguarded state-changing functions
description: The create() function uses _safeMint() which triggers the onERC721Received() callback on the serviceOwner if it is a contract. At the time of this callback, _locked = 2 (reentrancy guard active) protecting functions that have explicit guards (deploy, terminate, unbond, drain). However, update() and activateRegistration() do NOT have reentrancy guards. At callback time, mapServices[serviceId] already contains the newly created service in PreRegistration state. A malicious serviceOwner (if also the manager, or if the manager is set to the malicious contract) could call update() or activateRegistration() reentrantly during service creation.
message: If the manager address is a contract controlled by the attacker, they could reenter during create() to call update() or activateRegistration() on the newly created service before create() completes, potentially manipulating service configuration or immediately activating and paying deposits before expected.
recommendation: Add the reentrancy guard (_locked) to update() and activateRegistration() as well, or use _mint() instead of _safeMint() in the create() function.
exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker deploys a malicious contract M that is both serviceOwner and manager (or manager calls create with serviceOwner=M). 2. Manager calls create(M, ...). 3. _safeMint triggers M.onERC721Received(). 4. M calls update(M, newConfigHash, newAgentIds, newAgentParams, newThreshold, serviceId) or activateRegistration(M, serviceId) paying deposit. 5. Service state is modified mid-creation.

title: Composite key collision: serviceId bits overlap with agentId bits when serviceId > 2^32
description: The composite key serviceAgent = serviceId | (agentId << 32) is used for mapServiceAndAgentIdAgentParams and mapServiceAndAgentIdAgentInstances. If serviceId >= 2^32, the lower 32 bits of serviceId would overlap with the 32-bit agentId field (which occupies bits 32-63). For example, serviceId = 2^32 + X would set bit 32, colliding with agentId = 1 (which also sets bit 32). This causes two different (serviceId, agentId) pairs to map to the same storage slot, corrupting agent params and instance data.
message: When totalSupply exceeds 2^32 services, storage collisions in mapServiceAndAgentIdAgentParams and mapServiceAndAgentIdAgentInstances corrupt agent registration data, potentially allowing operators to register more agents than permitted or causing incorrect bond calculations.
recommendation: Use a hash-based key: uint256 serviceAgent = uint256(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(serviceId, agentId))). Or enforce a strict cap of 2^32 on totalSupply with an explicit check in create().
exploit_scenario: 1. Service with serviceId = 2^32 + 1 and agentId = 1: serviceAgent = (2^32 + 1) | (1 << 32) = (2^32 + 1) | 2^32 = 2^32 + 1. 2. Service with serviceId = 1 and agentId = 1: serviceAgent = 1 | (1 << 32) = 2^32 + 1. 3. Both map to the same key, causing storage collision.

title: Unchecked ERC20 Transfer Return Value in Token Distribution
description: In both `_distributeStakingIncentives` and `_distributeStakingIncentivesBatch`, the return value of `IToken(olas).transfer(depositProcessor, transferAmount)` is never checked. If the transfer fails silently (returns false instead of reverting), the deposit processor receives a bridge message expecting OLAS tokens that were never actually transferred. This can cause loss of bridged funds.
message: OLAS tokens may not be transferred to the deposit processor while the bridge message is still sent, resulting in staking contracts on L2 expecting funds that never arrive. The withheld amount accounting would also be corrupted since state was already updated.
recommendation: Check the return value: `bool success = IToken(olas).transfer(depositProcessor, transferAmount); if (!success) revert TransferFailed();` Or use OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20.safeTransfer().
exploit_scenario:
1. Call claimStakingIncentives() for a chainId with a valid stakingTarget
2. If OLAS.transfer() returns false (e.g., token paused or insufficient balance edge case)
3. _distributeStakingIncentives sends bridge message with transferAmount > 0
4. Deposit processor on L1 receives the call but has no OLAS to bridge
5. L2 staking contract never receives funds but mapLastClaimedStakingEpochs is already updated
6. Those epochs can never be claimed again

title: calculateStakingIncentives is Public and State-Modifying Despite Being Labeled for staticcall
description: The `calculateStakingIncentives` function is marked `public` (not `view`) and internally calls `IVoteWeighting(voteWeighting).checkpointNominee()` which modifies external contract state. The NatSpec comment says 'Call this function via staticcall in order not to write in the nominee checkpoint map', which is contradictory — the function DOES write to the checkpoint map via the external call. Any external caller can invoke this function to manipulate nominee checkpoints without going through the proper claim flow, potentially causing the checkpoint state to advance without corresponding incentive claims being processed.
message: An attacker can call calculateStakingIncentives() directly to advance checkpoint state in VoteWeighting for any nominee without those incentives being claimed or distributed. This can corrupt the epoch accounting for nominees, potentially causing them to lose unclaimed incentives if lastClaimedEpoch tracking gets out of sync with the actual checkpoint state.
recommendation: Make `calculateStakingIncentives` a `view` function and remove the `checkpointNominee` call from it, or move it to be internal-only and call it only from within the proper claim flow.
exploit_scenario:
1. Identify a nominee that has unclaimed staking incentives for multiple epochs
2. Call calculateStakingIncentives(numClaimedEpochs, chainId, stakingTarget, bridgingDecimals) directly
3. This calls checkpointNominee() in VoteWeighting, advancing the checkpoint
4. mapLastClaimedStakingEpochs is NOT updated (only the caller claimStakingIncentives updates it)
5. The next legitimate claim will use the advanced checkpoint with nomineeRelativeWeight returning different values based on the updated checkpoint state
6. Depending on VoteWeighting implementation, weights may be calculated differently than intended

title: claimOwnerIncentives Reverts When Both reward and topUp Are Zero
description: In `claimOwnerIncentives`, the variable `success` is declared but only assigned inside the block `if ((reward + topUp) > 0)`. If both `reward` and `topUp` are zero (no pending incentives), `success` remains `false` (default bool value). The subsequent check `if (!success) { revert ClaimIncentivesFailed(...) }` will always revert for zero-incentive claims. While this prevents zero-value claims, the critical issue is that `success` is also `false` if `withdrawToAccount` was never called, conflating 'nothing to claim' with 'transfer failed'. More critically, if `withdrawToAccount` returns `false` (indicating failure), there's no explicit handling — the revert message misleadingly says the claim failed when the real issue was a failed treasury withdrawal.
message: Users with zero pending incentives receive a misleading error. More importantly, if Treasury.withdrawToAccount() returns false (indicating a failed transfer), the contract reverts with ClaimIncentivesFailed but the reentrancy lock is properly released. However, the state in Tokenomics has already been cleared by accountOwnerIncentives() — meaning the user's incentives are wiped in Tokenomics but not received by the user.
recommendation: Restructure the success check: `if ((reward + topUp) == 0 || !success) { revert ClaimIncentivesFailed(msg.sender, reward, topUp); }` Or better: initialize `success = true` for the zero case and only set it based on withdrawToAccount result when called.
exploit_scenario:
1. User calls claimOwnerIncentives() when they have pending incentives
2. ITokenomics.accountOwnerIncentives() is called, clearing the user's balance in Tokenomics (returning reward/topUp values)
3. ITreasury.withdrawToAccount() fails and returns false
4. The function reverts with ClaimIncentivesFailed
5. Due to revert, mapLastClaimedStakingEpochs is NOT updated... but accountOwnerIncentives already cleared the Tokenomics state
6. Wait - the revert would roll back the accountOwnerIncentives call too since it's in the same transaction
7. Actually the concern is: if reward+topUp > 0 but withdrawToAccount returns false, the revert rolls back accountOwnerIncentives, so user can retry. This is safe.
8. The actual issue: if reward+topUp == 0, success=false, revert occurs — this is misleading but not fund-losing.

title: retain() Uses Imprecise Batch Division Instead of Per-Epoch Division
description: In `retain()`, the return amount is calculated as: `totalReturnAmount += stakingPoint.stakingIncentive * stakingWeight` across all epochs, then `totalReturnAmount /= 1e18` once at the end. The correct calculation should divide each epoch's contribution by 1e18 individually (as done in `calculateStakingIncentives`). Due to integer division rounding, `sum(a_i * b_i) / c` can be larger than `sum((a_i * b_i) / c)` when individual divisions truncate. This means `retain()` can return MORE tokens to inflation than the correct per-epoch calculation would produce, overcounting the refund.
message: The tokenomics inflation accounting is corrupted — more OLAS is 'refunded' to staking inflation than the actual weight-based allocation, allowing future epochs to distribute slightly more than intended. Over many calls to retain(), this discrepancy accumulates and inflates the staking budget beyond protocol parameters.
recommendation: Calculate per-epoch division: `totalReturnAmount += (stakingPoint.stakingIncentive * stakingWeight) / 1e18;` inside the loop, removing the final `totalReturnAmount /= 1e18`.
exploit_scenario:
1. Suppose 2 epochs with stakingIncentive=3 and stakingWeight=0.5e18 each
2. Per-epoch correct: (3 * 0.5e18)/1e18 + (3 * 0.5e18)/1e18 = 1 + 1 = 2
3. Batch division: (3*0.5e18 + 3*0.5e18)/1e18 = 3e18/1e18 = 3
4. Wait, that's the same. Try: stakingWeight=0.7e18 for epoch1, 0.3e18 for epoch2, stakingIncentive=1
5. Per-epoch: (1*0.7e18)/1e18 + (1*0.3e18)/1e18 = 0 + 0 = 0 (truncated)
6. Batch: (0.7e18 + 0.3e18)/1e18 = 1e18/1e18 = 1
7. The batch calculation returns 1 more unit to inflation than per-epoch, overcounting refunds

title: Missing Deposit Processor Validation Allows Zero Address Calls
description: In `claimStakingIncentives`, when `mapChainIdDepositProcessors[chainId]` returns `address(0)` (chain ID not configured or processor removed), the code calls `IDepositProcessor(address(0)).getBridgingDecimals()`. This will revert with an unhelpful low-level error. More critically, in `_distributeStakingIncentives`, if `depositProcessor` is `address(0)`, calling `IToken(olas).transfer(address(0), transferAmount)` could burn OLAS tokens (send to address(0)) before the bridge call fails. This results in permanent loss of OLAS.
message: If a deposit processor is removed (set to address(0)) for a chain ID that still has nominees with unclaimed incentives, calling claimStakingIncentives for that chain will attempt to transfer OLAS to address(0) before the bridge call reverts. OLAS tokens could be permanently burned.
recommendation: Add a check: `if (depositProcessor == address(0)) revert ZeroAddress();` at the beginning of claimStakingIncentives and in _calculateStakingIncentivesBatch before calling getBridgingDecimals().
exploit_scenario:
1. Owner calls setDepositProcessorChainIds([address(0)], [chainId]) to remove a deposit processor
2. Nominees still exist for chainId with unclaimed incentives
3. User calls claimStakingIncentives(epochs, chainId, stakingTarget, bridgePayload)
4. depositProcessor = address(0)
5. getBridgingDecimals() call on address(0) reverts — so OLAS is NOT transferred (calculateStakingIncentives is called first)
6. Actually the revert happens before transfer — but mapLastClaimedStakingEpochs is updated by calculateStakingIncentives
7. Wait: calculateStakingIncentives calls checkpointNominee and reads staking data, then claimStakingIncentives updates mapLastClaimedStakingEpochs BEFORE calling _distributeStakingIncentives
8. Epochs are marked as claimed, OLAS is minted to dispenser, then transfer to address(0) burns it

title: State Updated Before External Call Enables Epoch-Skip Attack via calculateStakingIncentives
description: In `claimStakingIncentives`, `mapLastClaimedStakingEpochs[nomineeHash] = lastClaimedEpoch` is written AFTER `calculateStakingIncentives` is called but BEFORE the distribution happens. If `calculateStakingIncentives` is also callable externally (which it is, being `public`), and it calls `checkpointNominee` on VoteWeighting, a sequence of calls can manipulate the checkpoint state relative to what epochs were computed for. Additionally, since `calculateStakingIncentives` itself doesn't update `mapLastClaimedStakingEpochs`, an external call to it between two legitimate claims in different transactions could cause weight calculations to use a stale checkpoint vs. what the dispenser tracks.
message: Weight calculations for nominees may be performed against a checkpoint that has been advanced by an external `calculateStakingIncentives` call, leading to incorrect incentive amounts being distributed or returned.
recommendation: Make `calculateStakingIncentives` internal or view-only, moving the `checkpointNominee` call into the claim flow explicitly.
exploit_scenario:
1. Nominee has unclaimed epochs E1, E2, E3
2. Attacker calls calculateStakingIncentives(1, chainId, target, decimals) — advances checkpoint in VoteWeighting to cover E1, but mapLastClaimedStakingEpochs remains at E1
3. User calls claimStakingIncentives(1, chainId, target, payload)
4. calculateStakingIncentives is called again for E1, but VoteWeighting checkpoint was already advanced
5. nomineeRelativeWeight for E1 may return different values now that checkpoint is in a different state
6. Incentive calculation is based on corrupted weight data

title: Incorrect Refund Calculation in unbond() After Service Update Changes Bond Amounts
description: In unbond(), the refund is calculated using the current bond parameters from mapServiceAndAgentIdAgentParams[serviceAgent].bond. However, update() can change bond amounts for agent IDs while a service is in PreRegistration state. If a service is activated, agents register bonds at one rate, service is terminated (going to TerminatedBonded), and the service owner had previously updated bond amounts before activation, the refund computed in unbond() uses the current (potentially different) bond params rather than what was actually paid. More critically, if an agentId is removed (slots set to 0) during a prior update(), its entry is deleted from mapServiceAndAgentIdAgentParams, so when unbond() tries to read the bond amount for that agentId, it gets 0, resulting in zero refund even though the operator paid real ETH.
message: Operators who registered agent instances for canonical agent IDs that were subsequently removed via update() will receive zero refund in unbond(), losing their entire bond deposit. Conversely, if bond amounts were increased after registration (impossible in current flow since update() requires PreRegistration state), operators could be refunded more or less than they paid.
recommendation: Store the bond amount at registration time in mapOperatorAndServiceIdAgentInstances (add a bond field to AgentInstance struct), and use that stored value in unbond() instead of looking up current params. Alternatively, ensure that bond changes cannot affect already-registered operators by only allowing updates when no agents are registered.
exploit_scenario:
1. Service owner creates service with agentId=1, bond=1 ETH, slots=2
2. Service is activated, operators register agents and pay 1 ETH bond each
3. Service is terminated → state = TerminatedBonded
4. Service goes back to PreRegistration (all unbond)
5. Owner calls update() removing agentId=1 (slots=0) → delete mapServiceAndAgentIdAgentParams[serviceAgent]
6. Service is re-activated and re-terminated with agentId=1 operators still bonded
7. When unbond() is called, mapServiceAndAgentIdAgentParams[serviceAgent].bond == 0 → refund = 0
8. Operators lose their ETH bonds

title: Key Space Collision in serviceAgent Mapping Key When serviceId Exceeds 32 Bits
description: Throughout the contract, a composite key is created as: uint256 serviceAgent = serviceId; serviceAgent |= uint256(agentIds[i]) << 32; This assumes serviceId fits in 32 bits (bits 0-31) and agentId occupies bits 32-63. However, totalSupply is a uint256 and serviceId is stored/passed as uint256 with no upper bound check. If serviceId >= 2^32, it will have bits set above bit 31, which will overlap with the agentId portion of the key. This causes different (serviceId, agentId) pairs to map to the same storage slot, corrupting agent parameters, instances, and potentially allowing double-registration or slot bypass.
message: If serviceId ever reaches or exceeds 2^32 (~4.3 billion), the composite keys for different services and agents will collide, leading to: wrong agent params being read, agents being registered to wrong services, slot limits being bypassed, or bond amounts being read incorrectly. An attacker who controls service creation timing could potentially exploit collisions.
recommendation: Add explicit bounds checking: require(serviceId <= type(uint32).max) and require(agentId <= type(uint32).max). Alternatively, use a proper nested mapping: mapping(uint256 => mapping(uint256 => AgentParams)) instead of the composite key scheme.
exploit_scenario:
1. Wait until totalSupply reaches 2^32 (serviceId = 4294967296 = 0x100000000)
2. Service A has serviceId = 0x100000000 with agentId = 1: key = 0x100000000 | (1 << 32) = 0x200000000
3. Service B has serviceId = 0x200000000 with agentId = 0: key = 0x200000000 | (0 << 32) = 0x200000000
4. These two different (service, agent) pairs share the same storage slot

title: Off-by-One in Slash Condition Causes Incorrect Slashing When Amount Equals Balance
description: In the slash function: if ((amounts[i] + 1) > balance) { slashedFunds += balance; balance = 0; } else { slashedFunds += amounts[i]; balance -= amounts[i]; }. The condition (amounts[i] + 1) > balance is equivalent to amounts[i] >= balance. When amounts[i] == balance (exact slash), the 'if' branch executes, which correctly zeroes the balance. However, the event emits amounts[i] as the slashed amount, while actually balance (which equals amounts[i]) is added to slashedFunds — this is consistent. The real issue: if amounts[i] == type(uint96).max, then amounts[i] + 1 overflows to 0, making 0 > balance always false (since balance >= 0), so the else branch executes: slashedFunds += type(uint96).max and balance -= type(uint96).max. If balance < type(uint96).max, this underflows. However Solidity 0.8+ reverts on underflow, so this would just revert. The actual vulnerability is that amounts[i] + 1 can overflow if amounts[i] = type(uint96).max, but since amounts is uint96[], this is bounded.
message: If the multisig passes amounts[i] = type(uint96).max, the addition overflows causing the condition to be false, then balance -= amounts[i] underflows and reverts. This could be used to DOS the slash function for a specific operator, preventing legitimate slashing.
recommendation: Replace (amounts[i] + 1) > balance with amounts[i] >= balance to avoid the overflow issue: if (amounts[i] >= balance) { slashedFunds += balance; balance = 0; } else { slashedFunds += amounts[i]; balance -= amounts[i]; }
exploit_scenario:
1. Service is deployed with operator having balance = 1 ETH (< type(uint96).max)
2. Multisig calls slash() with amounts[i] = type(uint96).max (2^96 - 1)
3. amounts[i] + 1 = 0 (overflow in unchecked context) BUT Solidity 0.8 will revert on overflow
4. Actually Solidity 0.8 reverts here, making slash() uncallable for this input
5. Malicious multisig could use this to prevent slashing

title: Missing Security Deposit Accounting: terminate() Does Not Zero securityDeposit After Refund
description: In terminate(), the security deposit is refunded to the service owner: refund = service.securityDeposit; (bool result, ) = serviceOwner.call{value: refund}(""); However, service.securityDeposit is never set to zero after the refund. The service's state transitions to either PreRegistration or TerminatedBonded. If the service goes to PreRegistration (numAgentInstances == 0), it can be re-activated via activateRegistration() which requires a new deposit equal to service.securityDeposit. The old non-zeroed securityDeposit value correctly represents the required new deposit, so this seems intentional. BUT: the securityDeposit value also represents ETH the contract 'owes'. If accounting is tracked anywhere expecting securityDeposit to be zero post-termination, this could cause issues. More critically, if terminate() is called from TerminatedBonded state (which the check prevents — it reverts for TerminatedBonded), this is fine. However the accounting of 'total ETH owed' = sum(securityDeposits for active services) + sum(operator balances) + slashedFunds is broken because terminated services still show non-zero securityDeposit.
message: Off-chain accounting tools or other contracts reading securityDeposit may believe the contract still holds those funds when they've been refunded. More critically, if any future function uses securityDeposit as a source of truth for ETH holdings without checking state, it could enable double-spending of security deposits.
recommendation: After the refund in terminate(), add: service.securityDeposit = 0; or alternatively track a separate 'deposited' flag. At minimum, document that securityDeposit represents the required deposit amount, not the currently held amount.
exploit_scenario:
1. Service created with securityDeposit = 1 ETH
2. activateRegistration() called, 1 ETH deposited
3. terminate() called (no agents registered), 1 ETH refunded to owner
4. mapServices[serviceId].securityDeposit still shows 1 ETH
5. Off-chain systems or future contract upgrades could incorrectly believe 1 ETH is still held
